title: When AI Takes Notes: Court Allows Privacy Claims Against Otter.ai to Proceed

reading.body:
An AI transcription service was sued for recording virtual meetings without obtaining consent from all participants. The system recorded conversations across multiple platforms by default and then used the recordings to train its AI models, practices the lawsuit alleges violated state and federal privacy laws. Whether the company actually obtained proper consent through its stated checkbox mechanism, and whether the recordings were genuinely de-identified before use in training, are contested in the legal proceeding.

The failure occurred at deployment: a system designed to record meetings was made the default behavior rather than requiring active opt-in from meeting participants. Catching this would have required either restricting the system to record only when all participants explicitly agreed, or implementing technical safeguards to prevent recording when participants had not consented. The lawsuit itself is an allegation; it has not established that consent was actually absent or that training on the recordings occurred.

Class-action suit claims Otter AI secretly records private work conversations
Otter.ai faces class action lawsuit for unauthorized meeting recording
Enterprise note-taking apps face legal scrutiny as Otter hit with privacy suit

summary:
A federal lawsuit filed in California accuses Otter.ai, a popular AI transcription service, of secretly recording private work conversations without proper consent. The suit, brought by Justin Brewer of San Jacinto, claims the company records virtual meetings on Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams by default without asking all participants for permission, then uses these recordings to train its artificial intelligence systems for financial gain. The lawsuit alleges this practice violates state and federal privacy and wiretap laws.

Otter.ai, which serves approximately 25 million users and has processed over one billion meetings since its 2016 founding, states in its privacy policy that it receives explicit permission through a checkbox users can select. However, the suit contends many users are still being deceived. Recent complaints on social media platforms describe instances where confidential information was shared without consent, including a case where sensitive business details were exposed to investors and another involving a human rights activist interview. The company claims it de-identifies audio before using it in machine learning systems, but the lawsuit questions whether this process effectively removes confidential information.
